medical.title: Injured e-scooter riders face higher risk of serious head or neck trauma than injured cyclists
medical.summary: Adults injured while riding e-scooters had a higher risk of serious head or neck injury than those injured on bicycles, even though their injuries were less severe overall, according to a national trauma-center analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons (JACS). Injured e-bike and bicycle riders, meanwhile, had similar risks of severe or critical injury after researchers accounted for differences in rider and crash characteristics.

medical.title: Semaglutide may improve eating disorder symptoms and body image in adults seeking obesity treatment
medical.summary: Adults receiving semaglutide for obesity treatment experienced greater improvements in several measures of disordered eating, eating disorder symptoms and body image concerns compared with participants receiving placebo, according to a new study led by researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The study was published in the International Journal of Eating Disorders.

medical.title: Study finds some BRCA2 gene changes carry lower breast cancer risk
medical.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers, in a study published in Nature Communications, have identified a group of BRCA2 gene variants associated with a moderate risk of breast cancer, a finding that could help health care teams better assess a person's cancer risk and personalize care.

medical.title: Mild Alzheimer's patients benefit from 40Hz sensory stimulation in national clinical trial
medical.summary: At the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston Nov. 16, MIT spinoff company Cognito Therapeutics announced the results of its pivotal clinical trial of a noninvasive, device-based approach to Alzheimer's disease (AD) treatment first discovered in The Picower Institute in 2014. The "HOPE" trial included 663 people in two "prespecified" subgroups of volunteers: those with diagnoses of mild Alzheimer's and those with moderate Alzheimer's.

medical.title: 'Perfectionist' as a label: Who claims it and who doesn't
medical.summary: It's a label people casually toss around in conversations about school, work and life in general: "perfectionist." But do young adults who call themselves perfectionists exhibit the behaviors and psychological traits associated with perfectionism?

medical.title: New study offers clues to how young neurons may help the brain form social memories
medical.summary: How does the brain remember someone we have met before, especially when new and similar experiences compete for our attention?

medical.title: Inspired by 'Flowers for Algernon,' experimental nose drops improve memory in mice
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Sydney have developed experimental nose drops that enhance learning and memory in aged mice while also preventing memory loss in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The treatment uses mRNA technology similar to that developed for use in COVID-19 vaccines.

medical.title: Chewable fish oil emulsion supplements may be better than soft-gel capsules
medical.summary: In a crossover clinical trial published in the European Journal of Lipid Science and Technology, investigators found that a chewable fish oil emulsion supplement may provide higher circulating levels of omega-3 fatty acids compared with a soft gel.

medical.title: Multiple short walks better than one long walk for controlling blood sugar
medical.summary: A randomized trial published in Obesity indicates that interrupting prolonged sitting with frequent brisk walks can improve blood glucose regulation to a greater extent than the same amount of walking performed as a single continuous bout.

medical.title: Nearly half of Australian health courses fail to mention sex and gender differences
medical.summary: Nearly half of Australia's accredited health and medical degrees do not mention sex or gender in a single course unit, according to a national review by the Center for Sex and Gender Equity in Health and Medicine at The George Institute for Global Health, despite extensive evidence that many conditions present differently in women, men and gender-diverse people.

medical.title: Medicare boost needed for Australia's 1.6 million cancer survivors
medical.summary: More than 1.6 million Australians living with and beyond cancer could benefit from proposed Medicare reforms to increase subsidized allied health visits, a move backed by new Flinders University–led research.

medical.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
medical.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

medical.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
medical.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

medical.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
medical.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

medical.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
medical.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

medical.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
medical.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

medical.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
medical.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

science.title: Greener living? It's all in the scheduling
science.summary: A research team led by Professor Inseok Hwang of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at POSTECH, including integrated MS-Ph.D. students Jeongwon Choi and Donghyeon Kang, has developed EcoTailor, a mobile planning system that suggests actionable low-carbon daily schedules tailored to users' commitments, transportation options and personal preferences.

science.title: Using a microwave link to transfer a three-level quantum state
science.summary: Quantum technologies, devices and systems that process, store, transfer or collect information leveraging the laws of quantum mechanics, could outperform their classical counterparts on some real-world tasks. Many of these technologies encode quantum information in qubits, which can exist in either of two basic states or a superposition of them.

science.title: Can natural soybean varieties handle dicamba drift? New study tests promising lines
science.summary: Some soybean growers who plant genetically modified dicamba-resistant soybeans have no intention of spraying the herbicide. Among other reasons, they're hedging against damaging dicamba exposure arising from neighboring fields.

science.title: Art experiments reveal artists' intuitive grasp of what makes images memorable
science.summary: Why do some artworks stick in our minds, while others fade away soon after we view them?

science.title: Sudden heat spikes harm honey bees more than sustained heat, study finds
science.summary: A sudden heat shock can be harmful to honey bees, but as a heat wave goes on, bees adapt and the high temperatures are less destructive.

science.title: Eagles preying on human-sized baboons upend existing evolutionary defense theory
science.summary: Researchers from the University of St Andrews have discovered that baboons the size of hominins (early human ancestors) are being preyed upon by eagles, reshaping the way scientists might think about predator–prey interactions during human evolution.

science.title: Climate change can worsen income inequality
science.summary: A study published in Sustainable Development that analyzed the relationship between climate change and income inequality for 23 emerging market economies from 2002 to 2022 found that greater climate pressure is positively associated with income inequality across three different inequality indicators (the Gini coefficient, the Palma ratio and the Theil index). Per capita income and institutional quality were negatively associated with inequality, whereas unemployment was positively associated with it.

science.title: Sierra Snow Season Spins Up
science.summary: A widespread, early-season snowstorm blanketed California’s mountains in white in mid-November 2026.

science.title: Houston leads large metros in child poverty, disconnected youth
science.summary: Houston is one of the nation's largest economic engines, but for many of its youngest residents, the path to financial stability begins with significant obstacles.

science.title: Photon fluctuations offer new way to probe electron dynamics in crystals
science.summary: Intense laser light can make a crystal emit new colors at frequencies many times higher than that of the original beam. This process, known as high-harmonic generation, provides a powerful way to investigate the rapid motion of electrons in solids. Researchers usually study the brightness and spectrum of the emitted light. Yet those measurements capture only part of the available information. Fluctuations between individual laser pulses can also reveal how the emission is produced.

science.title: New model reveals how water moves through tile-drained farm fields
science.summary: Tile drainage fundamentally alters how water moves through agricultural fields, affecting surface ponding, water-table dynamics, crop growth, nutrient transport and water quality. Yet fields with similar drainage systems can respond differently depending on soil, topography and tile design—differences that most models struggle to resolve at the field scale.

science.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
science.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

science.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
science.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

science.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
science.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.title: Injured e-scooter riders face higher risk of serious head or neck trauma than injured cyclists
mix_items.summary: Adults injured while riding e-scooters had a higher risk of serious head or neck injury than those injured on bicycles, even though their injuries were less severe overall, according to a national trauma-center analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons (JACS). Injured e-bike and bicycle riders, meanwhile, had similar risks of severe or critical injury after researchers accounted for differences in rider and crash characteristics.

mix_items.summary: Some soybean growers who plant genetically modified dicamba-resistant soybeans have no intention of spraying the herbicide. Among other reasons, they're hedging against damaging dicamba exposure arising from neighboring fields.

mix_items.title: Semaglutide may improve eating disorder symptoms and body image in adults seeking obesity treatment
mix_items.summary: Adults receiving semaglutide for obesity treatment experienced greater improvements in several measures of disordered eating, eating disorder symptoms and body image concerns compared with participants receiving placebo, according to a new study led by researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The study was published in the International Journal of Eating Disorders.

mix_items.title: Study finds some BRCA2 gene changes carry lower breast cancer risk
mix_items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers, in a study published in Nature Communications, have identified a group of BRCA2 gene variants associated with a moderate risk of breast cancer, a finding that could help health care teams better assess a person's cancer risk and personalize care.

mix_items.title: Mild Alzheimer's patients benefit from 40Hz sensory stimulation in national clinical trial
mix_items.summary: At the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston Nov. 16, MIT spinoff company Cognito Therapeutics announced the results of its pivotal clinical trial of a noninvasive, device-based approach to Alzheimer's disease (AD) treatment first discovered in The Picower Institute in 2014. The "HOPE" trial included 663 people in two "prespecified" subgroups of volunteers: those with diagnoses of mild Alzheimer's and those with moderate Alzheimer's.

mix_items.title: Art experiments reveal artists' intuitive grasp of what makes images memorable
mix_items.summary: Why do some artworks stick in our minds, while others fade away soon after we view them?

mix_items.title: 'Perfectionist' as a label: Who claims it and who doesn't
mix_items.summary: It's a label people casually toss around in conversations about school, work and life in general: "perfectionist." But do young adults who call themselves perfectionists exhibit the behaviors and psychological traits associated with perfectionism?

mix_items.title: Sudden heat spikes harm honey bees more than sustained heat, study finds
mix_items.summary: A sudden heat shock can be harmful to honey bees, but as a heat wave goes on, bees adapt and the high temperatures are less destructive.

mix_items.title: New study offers clues to how young neurons may help the brain form social memories
mix_items.summary: How does the brain remember someone we have met before, especially when new and similar experiences compete for our attention?

mix_items.title: Inspired by 'Flowers for Algernon,' experimental nose drops improve memory in mice
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Sydney have developed experimental nose drops that enhance learning and memory in aged mice while also preventing memory loss in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The treatment uses mRNA technology similar to that developed for use in COVID-19 vaccines.

mix_items.title: Eagles preying on human-sized baboons upend existing evolutionary defense theory
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of St Andrews have discovered that baboons the size of hominins (early human ancestors) are being preyed upon by eagles, reshaping the way scientists might think about predator–prey interactions during human evolution.

mix_items.title: Climate change can worsen income inequality
mix_items.summary: A study published in Sustainable Development that analyzed the relationship between climate change and income inequality for 23 emerging market economies from 2002 to 2022 found that greater climate pressure is positively associated with income inequality across three different inequality indicators (the Gini coefficient, the Palma ratio and the Theil index). Per capita income and institutional quality were negatively associated with inequality, whereas unemployment was positively associated with it.

mix_items.title: Chewable fish oil emulsion supplements may be better than soft-gel capsules
mix_items.summary: In a crossover clinical trial published in the European Journal of Lipid Science and Technology, investigators found that a chewable fish oil emulsion supplement may provide higher circulating levels of omega-3 fatty acids compared with a soft gel.

mix_items.title: Multiple short walks better than one long walk for controlling blood sugar
mix_items.summary: A randomized trial published in Obesity indicates that interrupting prolonged sitting with frequent brisk walks can improve blood glucose regulation to a greater extent than the same amount of walking performed as a single continuous bout.

mix_items.summary: Nearly half of Australia's accredited health and medical degrees do not mention sex or gender in a single course unit, according to a national review by the Center for Sex and Gender Equity in Health and Medicine at The George Institute for Global Health, despite extensive evidence that many conditions present differently in women, men and gender-diverse people.

mix_items.title: Houston leads large metros in child poverty, disconnected youth
mix_items.summary: Houston is one of the nation's largest economic engines, but for many of its youngest residents, the path to financial stability begins with significant obstacles.

mix_items.title: Photon fluctuations offer new way to probe electron dynamics in crystals
mix_items.summary: Intense laser light can make a crystal emit new colors at frequencies many times higher than that of the original beam. This process, known as high-harmonic generation, provides a powerful way to investigate the rapid motion of electrons in solids. Researchers usually study the brightness and spectrum of the emitted light. Yet those measurements capture only part of the available information. Fluctuations between individual laser pulses can also reveal how the emission is produced.

mix_items.title: Medicare boost needed for Australia's 1.6 million cancer survivors
mix_items.summary: More than 1.6 million Australians living with and beyond cancer could benefit from proposed Medicare reforms to increase subsidized allied health visits, a move backed by new Flinders University–led research.

mix_items.title: New model reveals how water moves through tile-drained farm fields
mix_items.summary: Tile drainage fundamentally alters how water moves through agricultural fields, affecting surface ponding, water-table dynamics, crop growth, nutrient transport and water quality. Yet fields with similar drainage systems can respond differently depending on soil, topography and tile design—differences that most models struggle to resolve at the field scale.

Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

mix_items.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
mix_items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

mix_items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

mix_items.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
mix_items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

mix_items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
mix_items.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

mix_items.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
mix_items.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

mix_items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
mix_items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

mix_items.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

mix_items.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
mix_items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

satire_ro.title: Bloc din Bucureşti, avariat grav după ce zeci de telefoane aflate în el au vibrat în acelaşi timp
